blocks.markdown:
## Why this paper matters

This 2017 paper introduced the **Transformer**, an encoder-decoder built from attention alone. Its claim is in the title: a model that turns one sequence into another, such as an English sentence into a German one, needs no recurrence and no convolution. It can be built from **attention** alone.

To see why that was a bold claim, start with what it replaced. In 2017 the leading translation systems were recurrent encoder-decoder networks (LSTMs and GRUs). A recurrent network reads a sentence one position at a time. It computes a hidden state $h_t$ from the previous state $h_{t-1}$ and the input at position $t$. That chain is the problem. You cannot compute $h_{50}$ until $h_{49}$ exists, so the positions *within one training example* must be processed one after another, however many GPU cores sit idle.

The usual workaround is to process many sentences side by side in a batch. The authors point out that this helps less as sentences get longer, because memory limits how many long examples fit in a batch. Tricks such as factorization and conditional computation made recurrent models faster, but the sequential constraint itself remained.

Attention was already familiar. Translation models used it to let the decoder look back at any source word, whatever its distance, but almost always as an add-on to a recurrent network.

Others had attacked the sequential bottleneck with **convolutions** (Extended Neural GPU, ByteNet, ConvS2S). These compute all positions in parallel. A convolution only sees a local window, though, so linking two distant words takes several stacked layers. The number of operations needed to relate two positions grows with their distance: linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. The authors cite work arguing that long paths like these make distant dependencies harder to learn.

The Transformer's bet is **self-attention**, attention that relates the positions of a *single* sequence to each other to build a representation of it. In one self-attention layer every word looks directly at every other word, so any two positions are a constant number of operations apart. The authors name one cost right away. Each output is an attention-weighted *average* of positions, and averaging blurs detail, which they call reduced effective resolution. Their fix, multi-head attention, comes later on this page. They believe the Transformer is the first transduction model built entirely on self-attention.

blocks.question: Recurrent models cannot parallelize across the positions of one sentence, so they process many sentences side by side in a batch. Why, according to the authors, does this workaround help less as sentences get longer?
options: Memory limits how many long examples fit in one batch, so less parallel work is available.
Longer sentences need deeper recurrent stacks, so each batch takes more sequential steps.
Long sentences produce vanishing gradients, so batch size must be cut to keep training stable.
Sentences of different lengths cannot share a batch, so long ones end up processed alone.
option_explanations: Right. The authors note that memory constraints limit batching across examples, and this bites hardest at longer sequence lengths, just where the sequential chain is longest.
The number of recurrent layers does not depend on sentence length; the sequential steps grow along the positions within a layer.
Vanishing gradients concern learning long dependencies, not how many examples a batch can hold.
Sentences of different lengths can share a batch; the paper itself batches sentence pairs by approximate length.
blocks.explanation: Within one sentence, h_t needs h_{t−1}, so the only parallelism left is across sentences. The authors point out that memory constraints limit that batching, and the limit matters most for long sequences. The tempting vanishing-gradient answer mixes up a learning problem with a hardware one.

blocks.markdown:
## The architecture

The Transformer keeps the familiar **encoder-decoder** shape. The encoder turns the input tokens $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ into continuous vectors $z=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$. The decoder then produces the output $(y_1,\dots,y_m)$ one token at a time. It is **auto-regressive**: each token it has already generated is fed back in as input for the next.

The **encoder** is a stack of $N=6$ identical layers, each with two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention, then a small feed-forward network. Every sub-layer is wrapped as
$$\text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{Sublayer}(x)),$$
which is a residual connection (the input added back to the output) followed by layer normalization. The addition only works if input and output have the same size, so every sub-layer and embedding outputs vectors of $d_{\text{model}}=512$.

The **decoder** also has 6 layers, with a third sub-layer in the middle that attends over the encoder's output. Its self-attention is **masked** so that a position cannot attend to later positions. The target sequence is also fed in shifted right by one. Together these guarantee that the prediction for position $i$ uses only outputs before $i$. During training the whole target sentence is available at once, so without the mask the decoder could simply peek at the answer. In the figure below, the encoder is on the left and the decoder on the right.

blocks.caption: Trace the two stacks. The left one (encoder) is repeated N×. Each layer is attention then feed-forward, each followed by an "Add & Norm" box. The right one (decoder) adds a middle attention block whose arrows come from the encoder. Notice also the "Positional Encoding" added at the bottom of both stacks and the "Outputs (shifted right)" feeding the decoder; both are explained below.

blocks.markdown:
## Attention itself

The paper describes attention as a soft lookup. A **query** is compared with a set of **keys**. Each key has a **value** attached. The output is a weighted sum of the values, and a value gets more weight the better its key matches the query. Think of a word asking "which other words are relevant to me?": its query is compared with every word's key, and it collects a blend of their values.

The Transformer measures the match with a dot product. With all queries stacked into a matrix $Q$, and keys and values into $K$ and $V$:
$$\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$
$QK^\top$ holds every query-key dot product at once. Softmax turns each row into weights that sum to 1. Multiplying by $V$ then mixes the values. The whole operation is a couple of matrix multiplications, which is why the authors call it much faster and more space-efficient in practice than **additive attention**, the main alternative, which scores matches with a small one-hidden-layer network. The two have similar theoretical complexity.

The new ingredient is the division by $\sqrt{d_k}$, where $d_k$ is the key dimension. Without it, additive attention beat dot-product attention when $d_k$ was large. The authors' explanation is a hunch they state as such: large dot products push the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients.

blocks.prompt: Take a query and six keys whose components are random, with mean 0 and variance 1, and use *unscaled* dot products. As the dimension d_k grows from 4 to 1024, what happens to the softmax weights over the six keys?
options: They spread out more evenly, as more dimensions average away the differences.
They stay about the same, since every score grows by the same proportion.
They collapse onto one key, while the other keys get almost zero weight.
blocks.resolution: They collapse. The dot product is a sum of d_k random terms, so its spread grows like √d_k, and the gaps between scores grow with it. A softmax over widely spaced scores puts nearly all its weight on the largest one. The widget below lets you watch this happen.

blocks.title: Why divide by √d_k?
blocks.instructions: The query and six keys here are **made-up random vectors** (components drawn with mean 0, variance 1, the assumption in the paper's footnote). They are not values from the paper. Move the **d_k** slider with scaling **off** and watch the weights pile onto one key as the raw dot products spread out. Then turn scaling **on**: dividing by √d_k keeps the scores on a similar scale at every dimension. The *gradient signal* readout is the sum of p(1−p) over the weights, a rough indicator of how much the softmax still responds to changes in its inputs. It falls towards 0 when the softmax saturates.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, explain why the Transformer divides the query-key dot products by √d_k before applying the softmax.
blocks.model_answer: A dot product sums d_k terms, so for random unit-variance components its variance is d_k and the scores grow with the dimension. Large scores make the softmax saturate, putting almost all weight on one key, and there its gradients become tiny, which hurts learning. Dividing by √d_k brings the variance back to about 1.

rubric.criterion: Explains that the dot products grow in magnitude (or variance) as the dimension d_k grows
Explains that large scores push the softmax into a saturated region with very small gradients, which hampers learning
Notes that dividing by √d_k restores a variance of about 1, independent of d_k

blocks.markdown:
A single attention step produces one weighted average per position. Recall the resolution cost: if a word needs both its subject and its object, one average blends them. **Multi-head attention** runs several attentions side by side instead. Each head $i$ first projects the queries, keys and values with its own learned matrices, attends, and produces its own output:
$$\text{head}_i=\text{Attention}(QW_i^Q,KW_i^K,VW_i^V),\quad \text{MultiHead}=\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1,\dots,\text{head}_h)W^O$$
Each head can therefore look for a different kind of relation, in a different representation subspace. The paper uses $h=8$ heads, each of size $d_k=d_v=512/8=64$. Because the heads are smaller, the total cost is about that of one full-size head.

The Transformer uses multi-head attention in three places:
- **Encoder self-attention**: queries, keys and values all come from the previous encoder layer, so every input position attends to every input position.
- **Decoder self-attention**: the same, except that each position may attend only to itself and earlier positions. The mask is applied inside the attention: the scores of illegal connections are set to $-\infty$ before the softmax, which gives them weight exactly 0.
- **Encoder-decoder attention**: queries come from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder output, so every output position can consult the whole source sentence. This plays the role attention played in earlier translation models.

blocks.caption: On the left, match each box to the formula: MatMul of Q and K, Scale by 1/√d_k, the optional Mask used only in decoder self-attention, SoftMax, then MatMul with V. On the right, see how h copies of that block each get their own Linear projections, and how their outputs are concatenated and projected once more.

blocks.question: During training the decoder receives the whole target sentence at once. What stops decoder position 3 from simply reading the very token it is meant to predict?
options: Scores to later positions are set to −∞ before the softmax, and the target is shifted right by one.
Scores to later positions are set to −∞ after the softmax, and the source is shifted right by one.
Later positions get a zero positional encoding, and the target is shifted left by one position.
Encoder-decoder attention reads only source words, and the target is fed in in reversed order.
option_explanations: Right. −∞ before the softmax gives later positions weight exactly 0, and the right shift means position 3's own input is the previous token, not the one to predict.
The mask has to act on the softmax inputs so that the remaining weights still form a proper distribution, and shifting the source does nothing about the target tokens the decoder reads.
Positional encodings only say where a token sits, and shifting the target left would place the next token at position 3 rather than hide it.
The decoder's own self-attention does read target tokens, and reversing their order would expose later tokens rather than hide them.
blocks.explanation: Two things work together. The mask sets illegal scores to −∞ before the softmax, so later positions get weight 0, and the outputs are offset by one position. So the prediction for position i depends only on outputs before i. A tempting wrong answer puts the mask after the softmax, but the paper masks the softmax inputs, so the weights over legal positions still sum to 1.

blocks.markdown:
Each layer also has a **position-wise feed-forward network**
$$\text{FFN}(x)=\max(0,xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2,$$
applied separately and identically to every position. It widens each vector from 512 to $d_{ff}=2048$ dimensions and back, with a ReLU between. Attention mixes information *across* positions; the FFN transforms each position on its own. Tokens become 512-dimensional vectors through learned embeddings. The input embedding, the output embedding and the final pre-softmax layer share one weight matrix, and the embeddings are multiplied by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$.

There is a gap, though. Nothing described so far knows about **order**. Attention compares every pair of positions in the same way, and the FFN treats every position alike. So the model adds a **positional encoding** to each input embedding, a vector of the same size that depends on the position:
$$PE_{(pos,2i)}=\sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}),\quad PE_{(pos,2i+1)}=\cos(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})$$
Each dimension is a sinusoid, with wavelengths ranging geometrically from $2\pi$ to $10000\cdot2\pi$. The authors hypothesized this makes it easy to attend by *relative* position, because $PE_{pos+k}$ is a linear function of $PE_{pos}$ for any fixed offset $k$. Learned position embeddings worked about as well. They kept sinusoids because these *may* extrapolate to sequences longer than any seen in training, a reason they give but do not test.

blocks.question: Suppose you want a trained Transformer to translate a sentence longer than any it saw in training. Which positional scheme do the authors expect to cope better, and why?
options: Sinusoids, because they are given by a formula at every position and may extrapolate beyond it.
Learned embeddings, because on the development set they scored clearly above the sinusoids.
Sinusoids, because their wavelengths stop at 2π, so positions past training simply wrap around.
Learned embeddings, because each has its own trainable vector and so adapts to unseen positions.
option_explanations: Right. This is the authors' stated reason for keeping sinusoids, though it is a hope ("may") rather than something they test.
The two versions performed about equally, so a score difference is not what separated them.
The wavelengths run from 2π all the way up to 10000·2π, so the encodings do not wrap around after a short range.
A learned embedding exists only for positions seen in training; a position beyond that has no trained vector to use.
blocks.explanation: Sinusoids are defined by a formula for any position, which is why the authors think they may extrapolate to longer sequences, whereas learned embeddings have nothing trained beyond the longest training position. The tempting answer that learned embeddings scored better misremembers the result: the two gave nearly identical results.

blocks.markdown:
## Why self-attention?

Section 4 makes the case in the abstract by comparing three layer types on three criteria. For $n$ the sequence length, $d$ the representation size and $k$ the convolution width, Table 1 gives:

| Layer | Cost per layer | Sequential ops | Max path length |
|---|---|---|---|
| Self-attention | $O(n^2\cdot d)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ |
| Recurrent | $O(n\cdot d^2)$ | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ |
| Convolutional | $O(k\cdot n\cdot d^2)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(\log_k n)$ |

**Sequential operations** measure how much must happen in order: the recurrent chain gives $O(n)$, while attention computes all positions at once. **Path length** is how many steps a signal travels between two positions. The authors cite work showing that shorter paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn. For attention, any two words are one step apart.

**Per-layer cost** is subtler. Self-attention compares all $n^2$ pairs, while recurrence does $n$ steps of a $d\times d$ matrix product. So self-attention is cheaper exactly when $n<d$. That is the usual case for translation: sentences of word-pieces are typically shorter than 512 tokens. For very long sequences the authors suggest restricting each position to a neighbourhood of size $r$, which costs $O(r\cdot n\cdot d)$ but lengthens the maximum path to $O(n/r)$. They leave this to future work. As a side benefit, attention weights can be inspected, a point the page returns to at the end.

blocks.prompt: Suppose you wanted to run a layer with d = 512 over a whole document of 20,000 tokens instead of a sentence. Using the per-layer costs from Table 1, explain how full self-attention compares with a recurrent layer here, and name the remedy the authors propose for such long inputs.
blocks.model_answer: Here n is far larger than d, so self-attention's n²·d cost per layer exceeds a recurrent layer's n·d²: comparing all 20,000×20,000 pairs becomes the expensive part. Self-attention still needs only O(1) sequential steps, though. The authors suggest restricting attention to a neighbourhood of size r around each position, which cuts the cost but raises the path length to O(n/r).

rubric.criterion: States that because n is much larger than d, self-attention's per-layer cost (n²·d) is now higher than the recurrent layer's (n·d²)
Names restricting self-attention to a local neighbourhood of size r as the authors' proposed remedy
Notes the trade-off that restricted attention increases the maximum path length to O(n/r)
Notes that self-attention keeps its advantage of O(1) sequential operations

blocks.markdown:
## Training and results

The models were trained on WMT 2014 English-German (about 4.5 million sentence pairs, a shared byte-pair vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens) and on the much larger English-French set (36M sentences, 32,000 word-pieces). Each batch held roughly 25,000 source and 25,000 target tokens.

All training used one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The **base** model took 100,000 steps at about 0.4 s each, 12 hours in total. The **big** model took 300,000 steps at 1.0 s each, 3.5 days.

The optimizer was Adam with $\beta_1=0.9$, $\beta_2=0.98$, $\epsilon=10^{-9}$. The learning rate followed a schedule:
$$lrate=d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5}\cdot\min(step^{-0.5},\ step\cdot warmup^{-1.5})$$
It rises linearly over the first 4,000 warmup steps, then decays with the inverse square root of the step number.

The paper announces three types of regularization but describes two headings. **Residual dropout** ($P_{drop}=0.1$ for base) is applied in two places: to each sub-layer's output before the residual addition, and to the sum of embeddings and positional encodings. **Label smoothing** ($\epsilon_{ls}=0.1$) trains the model against slightly softened targets. This makes the model less certain, which hurts perplexity, but it improved accuracy and BLEU.

blocks.prompt: The base Transformer trains for only 12 hours on 8 GPUs. On WMT 2014 English-German, how do you expect it to compare with the best earlier systems, including ensembles of several models?
options: It scores above every earlier system, ensembles included.
It roughly ties the best earlier single models but trails the ensembles.
It falls behind them; only the larger big model catches up.
blocks.resolution: Even the base model, at 27.3 BLEU, beats every previously published model and ensemble on English-German, at a fraction of their training cost. The big model widens the gap to more than 2 BLEU.

blocks.markdown:
Table 2 compares translation quality (BLEU on newstest2014, higher is better) and estimated training cost. On **English-German**, Transformer (big) reaches **28.4 BLEU**, more than 2 points above the best previous result, an ensemble. The base model's 27.3 already beats everything before it.

On **English-French**, the big model sets a new single-model state of the art at less than a quarter of the previous best model's training cost. Read the number with care: Table 2 lists **41.8**, while the text of Section 6.1 says **41.0**. The paper does not explain the mismatch. The big English-French model used dropout 0.1 rather than 0.3.

The cost column is an **estimate**, computed as training time × number of GPUs × an assumed sustained throughput per GPU (9.5 TFLOPS for a P100). By this estimate the base model cost $3.3\cdot10^{18}$ FLOPs, against roughly $10^{19}$ to $10^{21}$ for its competitors.

Two inference details matter for reproducing the numbers. The final model averages the weights of the last checkpoints (5 for base, 20 for big). Decoding uses beam search with beam size 4 and length penalty $\alpha=0.6$, settings tuned on the development set.

blocks.title: English-German BLEU on newstest2014, earlier systems vs the Transformer
blocks.caption: The earlier systems, ensembles included, sit between about 24 and 26.4. The single base Transformer clears all of them, and the big model sits more than 2 BLEU above the best ensemble.

blocks.prompt: The authors vary the number of attention heads while shrinking each head so that total computation stays constant (1 head of size 512, up to 32 heads of size 16). How do you expect BLEU to behave?
options: It rises steadily: the more heads, the better the translation.
It peaks at a middle number of heads and falls at both extremes.
It barely moves, since the total computation never changes.
blocks.resolution: There is a sweet spot. One head is clearly worst, 8 and 16 heads tie for best, and 32 tiny heads lose ground again, as the next block and chart show.

blocks.markdown:
To find out which components matter, the authors varied the base model one thing at a time and measured English-German on the **development set** (newstest2013), without checkpoint averaging. These scores are therefore lower than the test-set numbers above and should not be compared with them. The results are in Table 3:

- **(A) Heads**, at constant computation: a single head scores 24.9 BLEU, 0.9 below the best setting (25.8). Quality also drops with too many heads: 32 heads give 25.4.
- **(B) Key size**: shrinking $d_k$ hurts. The authors read this as a sign that judging compatibility is not easy, and that a richer function than the dot product might help.
- **(C) Size**: bigger is better. For example, $d_{\text{model}}=1024$ reaches 26.0, and $d_{ff}=4096$ reaches 26.2.
- **(D) Regularization**: without dropout, BLEU falls to 24.6, so dropout matters for avoiding overfitting.
- **(E) Positions**: learned positional embeddings give 25.7, against 25.8 for sinusoids, nearly identical.

The big configuration ($d_{\text{model}}=1024$, $d_{ff}=4096$, 16 heads, dropout 0.3, 300K steps, 213M parameters) reaches 26.4, against 25.8 for the 65M-parameter base model.

blocks.title: Development-set BLEU as the number of attention heads varies at constant computation
blocks.caption: Splitting attention into several heads helps a lot at first, levels off between 8 and 16, and turns down at 32 heads of only 16 dimensions each. The point at h = 8 is the base model.
blocks.source: Table 3, rows (A) and the base row

blocks.question: In Table 3 rows (A), 32 heads score 25.4 BLEU against 25.8 for 8 or 16 heads, at the same total computation. Which explanation fits what the page has shown?
options: Each head's keys shrink to 16 dimensions, and rows (B) showed that a smaller d_k hurts quality.
Thirty-two heads add far more computation, so 100K training steps are no longer enough to converge.
The 32 concatenated outputs exceed d_model, so the output projection W^O must discard information.
Thirty-two small heads saturate the softmax, since the 1/√d_k scaling is applied only once overall.
option_explanations: Right. At constant computation d_k = 512/32 = 16, and rows (B) showed that shrinking the key size hurts, which the authors read as compatibility being hard to judge.
Rows (A) hold computation constant: more heads means smaller heads, not more work.
Thirty-two outputs of 16 dimensions concatenate to exactly 512, so their shape forces nothing to be discarded.
The scaling sits inside each head's scaled dot-product attention, using that head's own d_k, so no head runs unscaled.
blocks.explanation: Because d_k = d_v = d_model/h, 32 heads leave each key with only 16 dimensions, and rows (B) showed that reducing the key size hurts quality. The tempting misreading is that more heads means more computation, when this experiment holds the total fixed by shrinking each head.

blocks.markdown:
## Beyond translation

To test whether the architecture is more than a translation trick, the authors tried **English constituency parsing**: turning a sentence into a bracketed tree of its phrases. They call it a hard case for three reasons. The output must obey strong structural constraints, it is much longer than the input, and RNN sequence-to-sequence models had not reached the state of the art when training data was small.

They trained a 4-layer Transformer with $d_{\text{model}}=1024$ in two settings: on the Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank alone (about 40K sentences), and semi-supervised with about 17M additional sentences. They tuned very little. Only dropout, learning rates and beam size were chosen, in a small number of experiments, and everything else was copied from the English-German base model.

The results are in Table 4. With WSJ only it scores **91.3 F1**, and semi-supervised **92.7**. The authors claim this beats all previously reported models except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar of Dyer et al. [8], which appears in Table 4 twice: 91.7 (discriminative, WSJ only) and 93.3 (generative). Table 4 also lists a multi-task model by Luong et al. at 93.0, above the Transformer's 92.7, which the paper's sentence does not mention. Notably, it beats the BerkeleyParser even with only the 40K WSJ sentences, which the RNN sequence-to-sequence model of [37] had not done.

Recall the side benefit from Section 4: attention weights can be inspected. The appendix shows encoder self-attention from layer 5 of 6. In one example, many heads attending from the verb *making* reach a distant phrase to complete "making ... more difficult". In another, shown below, two heads appear to resolve what *its* refers to, attending sharply to *Law* and *application*. Further examples show different heads doing visibly different things that seem related to sentence structure.

Take these for what they are: a handful of hand-picked examples. They suggest that heads specialize, which fits the case for multi-head attention, but the paper offers no systematic analysis.

The conclusion restates the main points. An attention-only model trains significantly faster than recurrent or convolutional ones, and it set a new state of the art on both WMT 2014 tasks. The authors plan to apply it to images, audio and video, to study local restricted attention for large inputs, and to make generation less sequential. Note that last goal: decoding is still auto-regressive, one token at a time.

blocks.caption: Look at the bottom panel: from the word *its*, the two heads put nearly all their weight on *Law* (its antecedent) and *application* (the noun it modifies), which the paper calls apparent anaphora resolution. Sharp, interpretable weights like these are what the authors mean by heads learning different tasks, though this is one sentence, not a measurement.

blocks.markdown:
## A critical look

The paper's own Table 1 contains its biggest long-term limitation. Self-attention's cost grows as $n^2$ in sequence length. That was harmless for sentences, but it became a central bottleneck once Transformers were applied to long documents, images and audio. A large body of later work on sparse, local and approximate attention grew out of this, essentially the "restricted attention" direction the authors flagged as future work.

Some claims rest on light evidence. That sinusoidal encodings "may" extrapolate to longer sequences is offered as a reason, not tested. The ablations are single runs on one development set, with no variance reported, so differences of a few tenths of a BLEU point, such as 25.7 vs 25.8 for learned positions, cannot be told apart from noise. The training-cost comparison relies on estimated throughputs for different GPUs, so it is a rough order-of-magnitude comparison. BLEU itself is an imperfect stand-in for translation quality. And the 41.0 vs 41.8 English-French discrepancy is never explained.

The attention visualizations are suggestive, but as far as I know later research has debated how far attention weights can be read as explanations of a model's decisions. Some later work also found the paper's arrangement of normalization after the residual addition sensitive to the learning-rate warmup, which led many later models to normalize before each sub-layer instead; I am less certain of the details there. None of this undercuts the central result: the architecture was adopted almost everywhere, including in encoder-only and decoder-only descendants such as the BERT and GPT families.

blocks.question: A colleague says: "The Transformer trains faster mainly because each of its layers does less arithmetic than an LSTM layer, whatever the input." Which account better fits the paper?
options: Its layers need O(1) sequential steps against O(n), so a sentence's positions run in parallel.
Its layers have O(1) path length against O(n), so each training update needs fewer steps.
Its per-layer cost O(n²·d) stays below an LSTM's O(n·d²) for inputs of any length at all.
Its attention is restricted to neighbourhoods of size r, so per-layer cost grows linearly in n.
option_explanations: Right. Removing the recurrent chain lets every position be computed at once, which is the paper's case for faster training.
Path length concerns how easily long-range dependencies are learned, not how many steps a training update takes.
Self-attention is cheaper only when n < d; for long inputs its n² term makes it more expensive.
Restricted attention is only proposed as future work; the trained models attend over all positions.
blocks.explanation: The paper's speed argument centres on parallelism: O(1) sequential operations against O(n) for recurrence. Self-attention also happens to be cheaper per layer when sequences are shorter than d, as they are for sentence-level translation, but that is conditional. So the colleague's "whatever the input" is false: for long inputs the n² term dominates. The path-length answer is tempting, but path length is the paper's argument about learning long-range dependencies, not about speed.

blocks.prompt: The authors say that relying on attention alone has a cost, which multi-head attention is meant to counteract. Explain what that cost is, how multiple heads address it, and one piece of evidence from the paper that heads help.
blocks.model_answer: Each attention output is a weighted average of many positions, so a single head blurs them together and loses effective resolution. With several heads, each with its own projections, the model can attend to different subspaces and different positions at once, keeping several relations apart. In Table 3, a single head scored 0.9 BLEU below the best multi-head setting at the same computation, and the visualizations show different heads doing different jobs.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the cost as reduced effective resolution caused by averaging over attention-weighted positions
Explains that multiple heads, each with its own learned projections, can attend to different information or positions in parallel instead of producing one blended average
Cites evidence from the paper, such as the Table 3 result that one head is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, or the visualizations of heads doing different tasks
Notes that the comparison holds total computation constant, or that too many heads also hurt
